newsitem.title: SOMALIA: Somali faction takes back towns, signs peace pact.
newsitem.headline: Somali faction takes back towns, signs peace pact.

text.p: A Somali faction led by Hussein Aideed has recaptured towns seized by clan rebels and has reportedly signed a peace pact with a rival faction in southern Mogadishu.

Residents of the towns of Hoddur, 300 km (200 miles) northwest of Mogadishu, and Wajid said by radio late on Monday that Aideed's forces retook both towns after fighting with the Rahanwein Resistance Army (RRA) and widespread looting.

Hoddur and Wajid, 90 km (55 miles) to the southwest, were captured by the RRA at the weekend and the RRA said at least 25 Aideed fighters were killed and 58 wounded. Residents said nine people were killed in the successful Aideed counterattack.
The RRA has fought a hit-and-run campaign against Aideed's forces since they seized the major southern major town of Baidoa in September 1995. Aideed's fighters captured Hoddur in January last year.
In southern Mogadishu, a radio station operated by faction leader Osman Hassan Ali Atto said on Monday he had signed a peace pact with Aideed following eight days of talks in Yemen.
Monitored by the British Broadcasting Corporation, the radio said a "peace declaration" called for an immediate end to armed hostilities, a ceasefire and an end to hostile propaganda.

It said both sides agreed to set up a committee to separate warring forces, remove roadblocks, reopen roads and ensure they observed the declaration. A reconciliation committee would also be established.
Atto was a former financier of Hussein Aideed's father, Mohamed Farah Aideed, and split with the main south Mogadishu faction chief in 1995 shortly before a U.N. troop pullout from Somalia.

Mohamed Farah Aideed died last August and was succeeded by Hussein Aideed, who was elected president of Somalia like his father by supporters. Many faction leaders including Atto reject his government.
Somalia has had no central government since the overthrow of late dictator Mohamed Siad Barre in 1991. A string of peace pacts have failed to end sporadic bursts of fighting, mainly in the capital.
